title: A curated list of Science Fiction Movies where Science is Key to the Plot

commenti.body: It's going to be hard to agree on a list. Terminator 2 and The Matrix are archetypical sci-fi movies but ultimately [guns and violence](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iuslUzbJEaw&t=86s) solve all their problems. Meanwhile the Halo TV show used sci-fi concepts like emotion suppressing drugs and genetics to drive the plot forward but felt like the generic lasers instead of bullets action you're complaining about.

How is Terminator 2 an example? There's no science in it at all, except as an excuse for the action. The same with the Matrix, which is far more philosophical than scientific.

I would say, if you can't even define what you're looking dor yourself with any accuracy or consistency then trying o get everyone else to agree is a bit of a lost cause.

Examples of Hard Sci-Fi should follow the following criteria:

1. The science is realistic, given an attempt at real-world explanations, and provided with hard rules within the film, which are not violated.
2. The plot of the film is about the science, either causing a scientific problem, searching for a scientific solution etc, not just window dressing for action
3. The protagonists are either scientists, civilians controlled by scientists, or have some significant scientific familiarity/respect.

Examples would be:

Twelve Monkeys  
Timecrimes  
Arrival  
Annihilation  
Interstellar  
The Martian  
Ex Machina  
Moon  
Gravity  
Deep Impact  
Sunshine  
Ad Astra  
Sunshine  
Primer  
Contact  
2001: A Space Odyssey

It would be made easier by holding to a primary criteria that science (or in-universe science) remains key to the plot.  
Though, I see what you mean.

For Terminator 2 the The Matrix trilogy, they share a similar premise about the fear of humanity losing control of their technology, and their in-universe science remained key to the plot throughout those movies.  
In regard to Soft and Hard Sci-Fi, they are both still sci-fi and not the issue of my proposal.  
The reason for my proposal is not "what is sci-fi?"  
The reason for my proposal is, that the sci-fi category is currently rendered meaningless by the mislabelling of lowbrow action movies as sci-fi, making it difficult to discover genuine and new science fiction – where the science is key to resolving the plot.

Sigh, I understand your question and I was indeed answering it. The problem is that clearly you either don't understand it yourself or not communicating it very well.

>For Terminator 2 the The Matrix trilogy, they share a similar premise about the fear of humanity losing control of their technology, and their in-universe science remained key to the plot throughout those movies.

No, the science isn't central to the plot at all in those films. They are the excuse for the plot, the window dressing.

In Terminator the resolution of the plot is in defeating the  superpowered villain and destroying them so well they can't come back. The resolution of the Matrix is pure fantasy, and philosophy, about self-sacrifice, fate, and free will. And kung-fu.

If you can't see that pretty fundamental distinction and are labouring under the idea that these are examples of films "where the science is key to resolving the plot", then there's probably no helping you.
I'm a simple man. I see Primer, I upvote!

Often, words which might superficially seem scientific words in a science fiction movie are actually techno-babble.  Some techno-babble words and sentences may sound more convincing than others; the consequences of some may be depicted as visuals in a more plausible and enjoyable way; but convincing speech or enjoyable visuals don't necessarily mean something is science.  He doesn't seem to understand that--and other things.  And that is just the beginning of what is or isn't central to a movie's plot (or as you put it, excuses for the plot).  And so on.
